# Local API v1

`GET /api/v1/diagnostics` requires pairing and returns a bounded local snapshot: running version, raw firmware if available, process-name check outcome and lengths, icon registration method, queue error categories and up to 64 session events. Startup events carry a stage, status and numeric result; transfer events carry HTTP/cURL codes when available. Loader version is `unknown` because Orbit does not detect it. Reports exclude arbitrary logs, process names, URLs, paths, titles and pairing credentials. Events reset when Orbit restarts; current queue statuses remain available. The UI copies the report only when requested and provides selectable text when the clipboard API is unavailable. Nothing is uploaded automatically.

Normal PS4 builds leave the process-name experiment disabled and report `not-checked`. Separate, best-effort `startup-status.json` and `startup-previous.json` records in Orbit's state directory retain the last startup/native-browser/listener-recovery stage across restarts. They contain only the version, timestamp, allowlisted phase/status and numeric result, and are not automatically exported by this API. Logging starts after the instance lock, so it cannot diagnose a failure in the ELF loader before `main`. An unavailable marker file does not prevent Orbit or its queue from starting. `listener-recovery` events report `started` when the HTTP daemon loses its listener or encounters a fatal poll failure, and `ok` once its replacement passes a poll cycle. Queue and pairing state remain in the same process.

Diagnostics also include a `storage` array with fixed drive IDs, `available` and a fixed `reason` for each inspected slot. It distinguishes an absent drive, an unmounted slot, an unreadable root, a read-only filesystem, unavailable capacity and an unusable `homebrew` destination. Discovery uses no-follow directory opens and checks device/inode identity; it does not use `access()` permission predictions. No filesystem paths or raw error messages are included. This is a fresh, read-only local inspection, not a write test. An absent `homebrew` folder is created only by a download action. New downloads and transfer starts (including resume/retry) verify creation and writing with an exclusive temporary file in the verified destination, unlinked before writing. A write failure rejects the download without hiding an otherwise accessible drive.

Download destinations are `homebrew` on `/data`, `/mnt/usb0` through `/mnt/usb7`, and `/mnt/ext0` through `/mnt/ext7`. The `ext1` slot is labelled **M.2 SSD**. Discovery must be able to open the root and any existing `homebrew` directory on the selected device. It does not require creation permissions on the mount root when `homebrew` already exists. Downloads require actual creation and writing in `homebrew`; if it is absent, the parent must permit creating it. Discovery creates nothing and excludes symlinks, read-only filesystems and unmounted slots. Queued jobs retain their original root/device/inode identity and cannot resume onto a replacement drive.

Served on TCP 34177. No CORS. Requests may use the console's numeric IPv4 address, localhost, or a hostname in `.home.arpa`, `.local` or `.localhost` that resolves to the console. Orbit does not configure DNS or advertise an mDNS name. Arbitrary internet domains are rejected. An explicit port must match Orbit's listening port. Every supplied Origin must match the request authority; API fetches marked cross-site or same-site are rejected. Mutation requests require JSON. Paired clients send `Authorization: Bearer <token>`; keep tokens out of logs and Git. The local-session endpoint still checks the actual loopback peer, not the hostname. HTTP is intended for a trusted local network; do not forward this port to the internet.

`/system` and `/updates` report `instanceId`, a random per-start identifier, not a credential. `/system.stopping` stays true while shutdown drains workers and saves checkpoints; API requests other than these two status reads return 503. The listener closes only after workers finish. Native restarts check the chosen saved/bundled version and the new instance before reporting success. Browser restart expectations persist in session storage for up to two hours and are checked in Updates & startup after reconnecting. Older services without an instance ID cannot confirm a process replacement. Connecting the native app to an existing service consumes its one automatic-start attempt, so an explicit Stop from another client is not undone by an automatic launch.

| Method / route | Authentication | Result |
|---|---|---|
| GET `/api/v1/system` | public | `platform` (`ps4`; `desktop` for the desktop build), pairing status, storage preference, state health, `httpPort`, `catalogueRevision`, and `launcherStatus` (`checking`, `ready`, `error`, or `not-included`). Orbit Zero reads `platform` to tell a PS4 from a PS5 and never sends a PS5's pairing to a PS4. `firmware` is the console's firmware (`"12.00"`; absent when unknown) and `ps4PackageFirmware` the newest firmware PS4 fake packages are built for (`"13.50"`) |
| GET `/api/v1/catalog` | public | Curated download options from enabled sources, with `gameId`, `platform` (`ps4` or `ps5`) and `sourceId`, without direct URLs; empty until sources are selected. Firmware facts, as labels only: `requiredFirmware` (`"10.xx"`, from a PS4 option's filename), `maxFirmware` (`"11.60"` on PS4 PKG/FPKG options) and, when the console's firmware is known and the option won't run on it, `firmwareIssue` (`ps4-package` or `newer-firmware`). Clients list those options last and never hide them |
| GET `/api/v1/catalog/updates` | public | Catalogue revision/count, last check, next automatic check, shared cooldown, cached/bundled state, busy state and refresh error; does not initiate network requests |
| POST `/api/v1/catalog/updates` | paired | `{action:"refresh"}` schedules a background refresh, returning 202; 409 while busy/unavailable, 429 during cooldown. The current catalogue remains usable. |
| GET `/api/v1/sources` | public | Enabled source IDs, acknowledgement status, notice version, and available source options with release counts and download readiness |
| POST `/api/v1/sources` | paired | `{enabled: ["archive", "vikingfile"], acknowledged: true, noticeVersion: 1}`; atomically saves source preferences and acknowledgement, pauses unfinished jobs from disabled sources |
| GET `/api/v1/session` | loopback only | Local console session, remote pairing code and `address`: the console's LAN IPv4 address for a phone to open (empty when there is no network route) |
| POST `/api/v1/pair` | six-digit code | Persistent client token; five failed attempts impose a 60-second cooldown. Orbit keeps 16 pairings, including the console's own session. When all are taken, a new pairing replaces the one unused for longest, never the console's own; that device gets 401 and pairs again. Last use is saved hourly in `state.json` as `tokenUsed` |
| POST `/api/v1/pair/show` | public, same-origin JSON | `{}` repeats the current code in a PS4 notification; returns only `{shown:true,retryAfter:30}`, never the code or a token. One request per 30 seconds across all clients; 429/503 responses include `retryAfter`. Desktop previews cannot send console notifications. |
| GET `/api/v1/storage` | paired | Accessible destinations on writable filesystems with `freeBytes`, `pendingBytes` and signed `projectedFreeBytes`; actual writes are checked on download actions |
| GET or POST `/api/v1/settings/extraction` | paired | `{deleteArchives, extractArchives}` (both default `true`). `deleteArchives`: whether a ZIP, 7z or RAR download is deleted once its files are extracted. `extractArchives`: whether ZIP, 7z and RAR downloads are extracted at all; when `false`, downloads added afterwards finish as the archive under its own name, need room only for the archive and report `keepPacked: true`. Queued downloads keep the choice they were added with. POST takes either or both. Also reported in `/system`. 400 without a boolean; 503 when it can't be saved. |
| GET or POST `/api/v1/settings/installation` | paired | `{deletePackages}` (default `false`): whether Orbit deletes a downloaded PKG or FPKG once the PS4 reports it installed. A failed or unconfirmed installation always keeps the file, and so does a file that changed after it was checked. Also reported in `/system`. 400 without a boolean; 503 when it can't be saved. |
| GET or POST `/api/v1/settings/ntfy` | paired | ntfy push notifications for the events chosen in `/settings/notifications`. POST `{enabled, server, topic, auth, username, password}`: `server` is an `http://` or `https://` address, `topic` up to 64 letters, digits, `-` or `_`. Without `auth` the username and password are forgotten; with it, an empty `password` keeps the saved one for the same username. Replies `{enabled, server, topic, username, hasPassword}`, never the password, which is kept in `ntfy.json` (0600) only. `ntfyEnabled` is also in `/system`. 400 for invalid values; 503 when they can't be saved. |
| POST `/api/v1/settings/ntfy/test` | paired | Sends a test notification with the saved ntfy settings, in the console's language, and waits for the server: `{sent:true}`, 409 without a saved server and topic, 502 with the reason when the server can't be reached or refuses it. |
| GET or POST `/api/v1/settings/notifications` | paired | `{console, downloadNotifications, events}`. `console` (default `true`; `downloadNotifications` is its 1.5.0 name and is still accepted) shows notifications on the console, in its system language. `events` chooses what the console and ntfy announce, all `true` by default: `downloadFinished`, `downloadFailed`, `installFinished`, `installFailed` (with what happened to the package) and `updateAvailable`, once per Orbit release. While `updateAvailable` reaches anyone, Orbit checks for releases itself ten minutes after starting and then every six hours. POST any of `console` and `events`, each event a boolean; others keep their value. `downloadNotifications` and `notificationEvents` are also in `/system`. 400 for unknown events or non-boolean values; 503 when they can't be saved. |
| POST `/api/v1/storage/preferred` | paired | `{storageId}` saves the drive new downloads start with (`preferredStorage` in `/system`); `""` clears it, so clients choose the first external drive. 409 when the drive is unavailable; 503 when it can't be saved. Creating a download also makes its drive the default. |
| POST `/api/v1/files/list` | paired | `{storageId, path}`: one folder of a drive (see [Files](#files)) |
| GET `/api/v1/files/status` | paired | `{operation}`: the running or last file operation, or `null` |
| POST `/api/v1/files/action` | paired | `{action, storageId, path, …}`: a new folder, rename, copy, move, delete, unpack, install or measure; pause, resume, cancel or an archive password for the running one. Returns `{operation}` |
| POST `/api/v1/files/link` | paired | `{storageId, path}`: `{url, name, sizeBytes}`, a download link for one file that lasts five minutes |
| GET `/api/v1/files/download/:ticket/:name` | the link's ticket | The file, whole or one `Range`; no pairing token (a browser's download can't send one). 404 when the link is unknown or expired, 409 when the file changed |
| GET `/api/v1/diagnostics` | paired | Local status, safe error categories and up to 64 session events; no remote requests or writes |
| GET `/api/v1/library` | paired | Current Library snapshot; schedules a read if no attempt occurred in the last 30 seconds. Returns immediately with `busy` while refreshing. |
| POST `/api/v1/library` | paired | `{}` requests a read of the provider's — or on a stock PS4 Orbit's own — installed-package inventory, subject to a shared five-second cooldown; returns the current snapshot. Does not trigger a scan or game action. |
| GET/POST `/api/v1/library/storage` | paired | Cached drive capacity and writable destinations; schedules a background read, with a shared cooldown. |
| POST `/api/v1/library/actions` | paired | Explicit `scan`, `mount`, `unmount`, `measure`, `copy`, `move` or `cancel`; returns 202 for an accepted command. Completion and errors are in the Library snapshot. `{action:"dismiss", jobId}` hides a finished copy or move result: `storageJob` is then `null` for every client, also after a restart, until the provider reports another job (409 while it still runs). |
| GET `/api/v1/downloads` | paired | Durable queue sorted by `order`, with saved title, progress and retry time |
| GET `/api/v1/art/:gameId/cover` or `/hero` | paired | The game's catalogue artwork, fetched and cached by Orbit for the TV app. 202 `{pending:true}` while it is being fetched; 503 while the artwork workers are busy or still starting (ask again shortly); 404 for unknown or hidden games and games without that artwork; 502 when every catalogue URL failed (retried after two minutes) |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/:id/move-up` or `/move-down` | paired | Swap position with the adjacent waiting job; active transfers remain fixed |
| GET/POST `/api/v1/history` | paired | Explicit file/history choices: settings, preview and removal; see below. Legacy history routes keep files regardless of the saved preference |
| GET/POST `/api/v1/power` | paired | Automatic shutdown status or `{enabled,jobId?}`. Disabled by default, 60-second cancellable countdown after new work finishes |
| POST `/api/v1/power/work` | paired | Zero reports `{busy,completed}` for its paired client; a disconnected busy client keeps shutdown blocked |
| POST `/api/v1/installations/files` | paired | Preview/delete a completed Zero transfer's downloaded source through its 32-character receipt origin. Never accepts an absolute path or uninstalls a game |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/:id/remove` | paired | Remove completed history or a cancelled job with no partial file; never deletes files |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/:id/delete` | paired | After confirmation, delete a cancelled download's partial file and remove its queue entry. An already-missing partial is success. Refuses unverified drives and other job states; completed files remain untouched |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/:id/forget` | paired | After a separate history-only confirmation, remove a cancelled entry without accessing any drive. Files remain, including on disconnected drives; a later download of the same file takes over an empty partial that no listed download has. Refuses other job states |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/clear-history` | paired | `{status:"complete"}` clears only completed history; `{status:"cancelled"}` clears only removable cancelled history. Omitting status retains the legacy combined cleanup. Kept partials and disconnected cancelled jobs remain |
| GET `/api/v1/favorites` | paired | Shared array of saved game IDs |
| POST `/api/v1/favorites` | paired | `{gameId,favorite:true\|false}` saves or removes a favourite atomically |
| GET `/api/v1/filters` | paired | Browse's saved filters, shared by every app: see [Saved filters](#saved-filters) |
| POST `/api/v1/filters` | paired | `{action:"save",name,page,filters}` or `{action:"delete",id}`; answers with the whole list |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads` | paired | `{releaseId, storageId, delivery?:"direct"\|"torbox"}`; direct is the default; returns created job ID |
| GET `/api/v1/archive-account` | paired | `{signedIn, name, busy}`: whether Orbit is signed in to Archive.org, and the account's screen name. Never the session or the email |
| POST `/api/v1/archive-account` | paired | `{action:"sign-in", email, password}` signs in to Archive.org and returns the status; `{action:"sign-out"}` removes the saved sign-in. 400 for invalid input, 409 when Archive.org refuses the account or a sign-in is already running, 502 when Archive.org can't be reached, 503 when it can't be saved (see [Archive.org sign-in](#archiveorg-sign-in)) |
| GET `/api/v1/viking-pass` | paired | `{saved, state, busy}`: whether a Vikingfile sign-in pass from another device is saved, and `state` `none`, `signed-in`, `signed-out` or `unknown` (not checked since Orbit started). Never the pass |
| POST `/api/v1/viking-pass` | paired | `{action:"save", pass}` checks the pass with Vikingfile and saves it only when Vikingfile confirms the sign-in; `{action:"check"}` checks the saved pass again; `{action:"forget"}` deletes it. Each returns the status. 400 for an invalid pass or action, 409 when Vikingfile refuses the pass, no pass is saved or a check is running, 502 when Vikingfile can't be reached, 503 when it can't be saved or removed (see [Vikingfile sign-in pass](#vikingfile-sign-in-pass)) |
| GET `/api/v1/debrid` | paired | Cached TorBox connection state, `available`, `busy`, safe error, cooldown and host/file-size availability; never returns credentials or account details |
| POST `/api/v1/debrid` | paired | `{action:"connect",apiKey}` validates and saves a TorBox connection asynchronously; `{action:"refresh"}` checks account/host availability; `{action:"disconnect"}` removes the key and pauses unfinished TorBox jobs. Returns 202, 409 while checking, 429 during cooldown; no remote file deletion |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/:id/pause` | paired | Interrupt active transfer, preserving its partial file |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/:id/resume` or `/retry` | paired | Revalidate original storage and source, then queue |
| POST `/api/v1/downloads/:id/cancel` | paired | Preserve partial by default; `{deletePartial:true}` deletes only that partial |
| GET `/api/v1/updates` | paired | Running/saved/latest versions, progress, error, cooldown and restart requirement; `selfRestart` for the supported ELF-loader restart path (false after a failed connection, not a live reachability probe), `activationState` (`running`, `saved` or `restarting`) and `restartNotice` for an unsuccessful automatic restart, `updateAll` and `tvAppUpdated` for the last `update-all`; no network request or writes |
| POST `/api/v1/updates` | paired | `{action:"check"}` starts a background check. `{action:"install",version,checksum}` installs the checked candidate (expires after 15 minutes). `{action:"stop",confirmed:true}` saves a paused queue and stops only Orbit after responding; add `resume:true` when a client starts Orbit again itself, and the downloads it paused continue after the restart. `{action:"restart",confirmed:true}` first connects to the ELF loader on port 9021. When 9021 refuses the connection, it sends Orbit's saved elfldr (`/data/orbit-store/elfldr.elf`) to GoldHEN's payload loader on 9090 and waits up to 20 seconds for 9021; GoldHEN's loader never gets Orbit itself and is never contacted without that file (409 when no loader can be reached, and Orbit keeps running). It then stops like `stop`, sends the saved copy to that connection and marks the downloads it paused to continue after the restart. A saved copy older than the running one is never sent, so the running version is used; the new process waits up to 15 seconds for the old one's lock and port. `{action:"update-all",serviceVersion,serviceChecksum,tvAppVersion,tvAppChecksum}` installs the checked releases it names (either pair may be left out; each check expires after 15 minutes): the TV app first, then Orbit, which then restarts as above, or stays saved for a manual restart without a loader. Its phases are `tv-app`, `downloading`, `saving`, then `restarting`, `updated` (TV app only) or `saved`. Returns 202; 409 while busy, stale or unavailable; 429 during cooldown. |
| GET `/api/v1/tv-app` | paired | The detected native app and `installedPath` on internal, USB or extended storage (`installed`: `none`, `orbit`, `manual`, `folder` or `blocked`), the installed and latest TV app versions, the `serviceVersion` that release carries (empty when the feed doesn't say), progress, error and cooldowns; no network request or writes. `{available:false}` in desktop previews |
| POST `/api/v1/tv-app` | paired | `{action:"check"}` recovers an existing TV install task if one is pending, otherwise reads the TV app feed; add `automatic:true` when the TV app opens (shares a six-hour cooldown, like Orbit's own updates). `{action:"install",version,checksum}` downloads and installs the checked release (expires after 15 minutes); add `replace:true` to replace a copy the owner placed. Returns 202; 409 while busy, stale or unavailable, or when another copy blocks the install; 429 during cooldown; 507 without space on the TV app’s destination drive |
| GET `/api/v1/tv-app/look` | paired | `{look}`: the TV app's own choices (interface, language, accent and the like) as the JSON text the app saved, or `null` when it never sent any. A freshly installed or updated TV app reads it before its first screen |
| POST `/api/v1/tv-app/look` | paired | `{look:"<JSON object as text>"}` up to 16 KB, sent by the TV app whenever its choices change; kept in `/data/orbit-store/tv-app-look.json`. Returns `{saved:true}`; 400 for anything that isn't a JSON object or is larger |
| GET `/api/v1/autoboot` | paired | Saved runtime and, per payload manager, whether it is installed, lists Orbit and is managed by Orbit; `goldHEN` reports `installed`, AutoRun `enabled`, and config `readable`. `{available:false}` in desktop previews |
| POST `/api/v1/autoboot` | paired | `{manager:"payload-manager",enabled}` edits only Orbit’s GoldHEN AutoRun entry. Enabling requires integration consent; invalid/unreadable config is rejected. Unsupported manager names return 404 |
| POST `/api/v1/integrations` | paired | `{manager: "payload-manager" \| "homebrew-launcher", enabled}`; persist opt-in copying of Orbit's starter (`launcher/starter.c`, which starts the saved service) to GoldHEN's `/data/payloads` LaunchPad list or the Homebrew Launcher folder. Returns the manager status. |

Paired clients can manage files within supported drive roots through Files, and explicitly install validated packages through the installation APIs. Files rejects path traversal, symlinks, protected Orbit data and files used by active operations. Confirmed deletion removes the selected file or folder; it does not uninstall an installed title. A scan may cause a compatible provider to register or mount games. Manager integration writes only Orbit's own copies; see [installation](installation.md). Production host previews of the Store backend reject game-transfer creation. Test-only fixture URLs are not available in production payloads.

In the 1.7.5 implementation, an optional `contentFormat: "LZ4"` labels source-classified PS4 LZ4 game archives without changing their legacy `format`, `compression`, or archive inspection requirements. It is retained in queue snapshots and transfer context. See [Compressed options](catalogue.md#compressed-options).

The catalogue remains a flat list of download options at the API boundary. Each option has its own unique `id`, plus a stable curated `gameId` shared across its source, format, version, and regional variants. The storefront groups by `gameId` into one card per game, then lists the enabled options inside that game's page. Title strings and regional title IDs are not grouping keys. Download requests and queued jobs use the chosen option's `id` as `releaseId`, preserving existing queue identities. The current build permits up to 8,192 options, plus the separate diagnostic release. Catalogue envelopes are limited to 16 MiB; older compatibility feeds retain their 4,096-option and 8 MiB limits.

The source list is fixed: `archive`, `vikingfile`, `akirabox` and `datanodes`. `enabled` can contain any subset. Unknown or repeated IDs, a missing acknowledgement, or a mismatched notice version return 400. Settings persistence failures return 503 without applying the new choices. Game creation and resume/retry return 409 when the game's source is disabled or the current notice is unacknowledged. A selected source still needs a supported option: browser-only pages require the PS4 browser flow for direct delivery, or a connected TorBox account that supports that host and file size. The pinned diagnostic release is independent of game-source selection.

TorBox status reports Archive.org, Vikingfile and DataNodes separately. Availability and limits come from TorBox's host response; a missing or unavailable host cannot be queued through TorBox. DataNodes submissions use the validated permanent `browserUrl` when present, preserving that identity through pause, restart and temporary-link renewal. AkiraBox is not offered through TorBox.

Source choices and the acknowledgement version/timestamp are stored with the queue and apply to all clients. First use, legacy state without source settings, and an outdated notice require a new acknowledgement; no source is silently enabled. Disabling a source pauses active, queued, and retrying transfers and preserves their files. Re-enabling it does not automatically resume them. Completed files are unaffected. There is no library import or arbitrary source URL endpoint.

State is stored atomically under `/data/orbit-store`. Users can choose 1–8 simultaneous game downloads, with one as the default, sharing up to 64 connections. The queue retains up to 100 jobs and 16 paired-client slots. Interrupted running jobs become paused after restart; already queued jobs remain queued only when their source is enabled and acknowledged. Pairing codes rotate when the payload restarts. Saved paired-client tokens remain valid. Revoke all pairings by stopping Orbit and removing only the `tokens` array from its state file using a trusted maintenance tool.

**Pair devices** in the storefront header opens a persistent code display on the console, refreshed each time the panel opens. On a phone or computer, **Show code on PS4** repeats the notification without restarting Orbit or changing the current code, paired devices, or download queue. `pairNotificationAvailable` in `/system` indicates whether this action is supported.

Game fields (`publisher`, `releaseDate`, `cover`, `hero`, `coverFallback`, `heroFallback`, `artworkLayout`) are joined from the shared metadata snapshot during the offline build. Card covers try `coverFallback` only after the primary fails. Backgrounds load separately: the CDN cover provides an immediate ambient layer, while a distinct publisher banner from `hero` (wide layout) or `heroFallback` (ambient layout) loads above it. Only a wide image becomes the full banner; blocked, unavailable or square alternatives leave the ambient layer visible. Every option for the same `gameId` receives identical game metadata. `sourceCheckedAt` records desktop metadata/HEAD/range verification, separately from `consoleVerified`.

`publisher`, `releaseDate`, `genre`, `tagline` and `description` can be null when unsourced. Clients omit those details. Title, cover, hero and artwork layout remain required. Discover sorts dated games newest first and leaves undated or future-dated games in All games. Catalogue refresh keys include `catalogueRevision`, server version and source settings, so a running client notices metadata changes even when the game count stays the same.

Update/reinstall reads only the fixed Orbit release feed and downloads the selected official ELF over verified HTTPS. It checks SHA-256 and ELF64/x86-64 headers before replacing files. Redirects outside GitHub release hosts, oversized responses and older versions are rejected. Install supports the same version for repair. The running instance remains active until the user confirms Stop Orbit, then the saved ELF must be started through a payload manager. A partially failed refresh of payload-manager copies remains an error; it is never reported as a successful install. Updater state is process-local except the saved version record; the saved version survives restart.

Catalogue updates use the fixed official feed, independent of ELF releases. Startup and six-hour background checks validate and atomically cache newer revisions. Feed generations have separate compatibility rules: after an app upgrade, the current feed can replace an older-generation cache at the same revision. Changes within the same generation still require a new revision, and older revisions are rejected. Legacy caches remain available offline until a valid replacement arrives. Migration replaces only the catalogue cache; saved downloads, pairing, source choices and account settings are retained. Persisted jobs include their original release identity; a catalogue replacement cannot change the file or destination of an existing job. See [catalogue publishing](catalogue.md#publish-catalogue-changes-without-an-elf-update).

Queue order changes only order fields; a transfer's fixed in-memory job slot never moves. Cleared slots are reusable within the 100-job limit. Legacy history-cleanup endpoints preserve completed files and refuse to orphan cancelled partials. Current clients use the explicit `/history` preview/removal flow described below. Source choices, queue order and favourites survive restart. Favourites remain saved when a source is disabled or a title temporarily disappears.

**Delete download** in Cancelled removes the partial and the entry in one action. The writer must already be stopped. A manually deleted partial (`ENOENT`) is treated as already removed; permission, filesystem and other errors leave the entry available for retry. Legacy remove-history and bulk-cleanup endpoints keep files regardless of the saved preference. Current clients use `/history` to explicitly choose keep or delete, including reviewed deletion of completed source files. They do not uninstall games or delete remote TorBox cache items; see [Removing history and downloaded files](#removing-history-and-downloaded-files).

A cancelled record with a missing partial on its verified original drive can be replaced by a fresh download. If reconnecting changes the drive identity, a fresh download may instead create a new job pinned to the currently selected drive, retaining the old cancelled record for recovery. Both final and partial paths must be confirmed absent, and the full download must fit; errors reading either path fail closed. The old job cannot resume or delete files on an unverified drive. This behavior applies to direct, captured Vikingfile and TorBox creation.

A drive the console remounts, for example after repairing it, keeps its path and files but gets new device numbers. Orbit writes a 32-digit random mark to `.orbit-drive` at the top of each drive it downloads to, saves it with the job as `driveMark`, and adds it to unfinished jobs saved before marks existed. Before resuming, refreshing a link, deleting a partial or removing a record, a job whose drive does not match is re-checked: the drive at its saved path must carry the same mark, when the job has one, and must hold the job's own `.part` file with at least its saved progress, or no such file when nothing was saved. Then the job takes the new device numbers. Otherwise the drive is still unverified and the job stays blocked.

`pendingBytes` sums additional disk space needed for unfinished jobs on the same original drive identity, including paused/failed jobs and excluding completed/cancelled jobs. Already-written partial bytes are reflected in filesystem free space. For segmented files, allocated blocks may also include unwritten gaps; those reduce additional space needed but never count as download progress. `projectedFreeBytes = freeBytes - pendingBytes`; a negative value is a shortfall. Creation and resume check the whole plan with a 16 MiB safety margin. Estimates are snapshots; other applications can change actual free space.

`addedAt` is an optional timezone-qualified catalogue addition timestamp, independent of `releaseDate`. Legacy feeds without it still load. Browse uses `releaseDate` for its default newest-first order, with undated games last.

Transfers validate the final file response after HTTP redirects. Intermediate HTML redirect responses do not produce a page error or carry their `Retry-After` value into later responses. The final response still must pass content-type, size, range and saved-identity checks before bytes are written.

New downloads with at least 32 MiB remaining, an unfinished first eighth and a strong ETag can use the configured connection count (eight by default). A one-byte GET first confirms exact byte-range support. A valid full-file 200 response falls back to one connection; small files and sources without a strong ETag also use one. Existing partials keep their range layout on resume. The configured simultaneous-game limit applies, with a shared 64-connection budget and at most eight connections per TorBox game. A short interrupted HTTP 206 range retries from its saved position without restarting the other ranges. Provider retry/backoff limits still apply to the whole job. An existing parallel partial requires valid ranges on resume; if the provider stops supporting them, Orbit preserves the partial and reports an error.

Network callbacks copy accepted data into an 8 MiB bounded buffer, divided across the active ranges. A separate disk writer coalesces chunks into writes of up to 256 KiB (short tails flush within roughly 50 ms), checks drive identity, and performs periodic and final checkpoints. The network can continue filling available buffer space while the writer flushes data and saves state. Full buffers apply backpressure. Pause, cancel, network failures and shutdown stop new input, join the writer, and preserve only durable progress before changing the job status or deleting its partial file. Write/flush failures abort the attempt; uncheckpointed data is overwritten on resume.

A reviewed compressed option (`compression` is `zip`, `7z` or `rar`, with `extractedBytes`) downloads to the usual partial file, is verified, then has status `waiting-extraction` while another archive owns the extraction worker. Once that worker becomes available, it has status `inspecting` for an unidentified archive or `extracting` while its files are written into a private `homebrew/.orbit-extract-<job>` folder. Jobs report `extracted`, `extractTotal`, `output` (the published name) and `archiveKept`, and `path` points at the output. A restart during extraction pauses the job; resuming repeats only the extraction. Queues holding a compressed job are saved as schema 6, which older payloads reject rather than mistaking the archive for a finished file. Space checks reserve the archive and its extracted size together.

Completed and extracted jobs expose known `requiredFirmware`, `maxFirmware`, `firmwareIssue`, `firmwareSource` and `consoleFirmware` fields when available. After extraction, a bounded scan reads supported `sce_sys/param.json` metadata; absent or invalid metadata does not establish compatibility. The PS4 PKG/FPKG upper firmware limit still takes precedence where applicable. These fields are advisory and do not block download or installation. Extracted jobs also expose `backport: true` when the bounded scan finds a `fakelib` or `fakelib2` directory. This means backport files were found, not that compatibility is confirmed; clients show placement instructions without moving those files.

Queue state schema 4 records one, two or four equal partitions in `rangeReceived`. Each cursor advances only after the sole writer successfully flushes the file. Persisted `received` is their sum, including when another API action saves queue state during a transfer; live API progress may be ahead of the checkpoint. The layout is saved before any buffered writes. Neither file length nor bytes waiting in memory prove completion. Schema 1 contiguous partials retain their prefix, and schema 2 partials retain their two ranges. This tester also accepts legacy schema-3 TorBox queues with two saved ranges and migrates them to schema 5. Schema 5 uses the same durable range layout as schema 4 plus TorBox delivery identity. Older payloads reject schema 4. Keep using 0.7.0 or later after upgrading. Migration creates an exact private backup of the previous queue before writing the new schema; the backup is for rollback, not for resuming downloads started afterward. Invalid range maps or shorter-than-recorded partials fail closed. Source identity, full-size validation and the catalogue checksum (when provided) still apply before finalizing.

`GET /api/v1/diagnostics` includes a `writer` object per download with measurements from its last finished transfer attempt: `peakBufferedBytes`, `writeCalls`, `syncCalls`, `bufferWaitSeconds`, `writeSeconds` and `syncSeconds`. These are session-only counters with no URLs, paths or credentials; `syncSeconds` measures file flushes, excluding queue-state serialization. Local test builds accept `ORBIT_TEST_CONNECTIONS=2` or `4` for comparisons; production defaults to eight. `make benchmark-transfer` compares two and four against the same bounded loopback fixture; it does not measure PS4 or provider performance.

TorBox jobs use schema 5 and retain their original catalogue identity plus a private account hash and remote item/file IDs. `delivery` and `deliveryPhase` are public queue fields; keys, account hashes and temporary download URLs are not. New submission pacing is durable in `debridNextCreate`, and each job's last submission time in `debridSubmittedAt`. Credentials live separately in a mode-0600 `debrid.json`, while signed addresses exist only during a transfer attempt. See [TorBox downloads](debrid.md) for connection, recovery and downgrade behavior.

Since 0.0.3, `/debrid` status includes `alwaysUseTorBox` and `lastDelivery` (`direct` or `torbox`). `POST /debrid` with `{action:"preferences",alwaysUseTorBox:true|false}` persists the override. New download requests use that override first, then an explicit delivery choice, then the remembered choice. Existing jobs retain their delivery method.

Library is independent of the download catalogue and source settings. Its response includes `status`, `message`, `provider`, `providerVersion`, `busy`, `stale`, Unix-second `checkedAt`/`updatedAt`, `refreshAfter` in seconds, and `games`. Status is `idle`, `ready`, `unavailable`, `unsupported` or `error`; a successful empty inventory is `ready` with an empty array. Entries contain `titleId`, `title`, `platform`, `format`, `path`, `runtimePath`, `location`, independent `installed`/`mounted`/`onDrive` booleans, nullable `installedSizeBytes`, and optional catalogue `cover`. `foundByOrbit:true` marks a game installed from a PKG that the running provider does not list and Orbit found itself. Counts may overlap. A failed read preserves the last valid in-memory snapshot with `stale:true`; it does not infer that sources were deleted. This cache ends when Orbit stops.

The Library worker queries `127.0.0.1` on the configured provider API port (default 10101). It respects `/data/shadowmount/config.ini` without changing it, rejects redirects and unsupported schemas, bounds replies to 8 MiB and 4,096 titles, and keeps provider calls off HTTP request threads. Production desktop previews never contact a provider. When no provider answers — always the case on a stock PS4 — Orbit serves the inventory itself: it reads the console's app folders (`/user/app` and the `/mnt/ext0` and `/mnt/ext1` app folders) for title folders containing a regular `app.pkg`, each game's `param.sfo` or `param.json` for its name, and its own storage checks for drive capacity. Local mode reports `provider:"Orbit"`, capabilities `list_games` and `rescan`; mount, unmount, copy, move and storage-job actions stay unavailable. No private socket, arbitrary URL or general-purpose uninstall route is exposed. Library moves use the supported, narrowly scoped source-deletion endpoint only after verifying the destination.

Snapshot additions: `capabilities`, `action` (request ID, action, title ID, queued/running/complete/error state and message), `storageJob`, `storageBusy`, `storageError`, and the automatic work under way: `scanning` (a scan was just requested, by Orbit or by you, and Orbit is reading what the provider registers — or on a stock PS4 re-reading its own inventory) and `measuring` (game sizes are being measured). Game rows add `sourceKey`, `managed`, `canManageSource`, nullable `sizeBytes` and `sizeStatus`. Missing optional management fields disable mutations for that row. Orbit measures source sizes itself, using `games` with `include_size:true`, when games without a size appear; sizes are cached by source identity. The `measure` action still measures on request. Automatic scans and measures never change `action`. See [automatic updates](library.md#automatic-updates-and-artwork).

Storage replies contain normalized `drives`, `destinations`, `busy`, `stale`, `updatedAt`, and `error`. Rows have an opaque `id`, path/mount point, label, filesystem, read-only flag, total/free/used bytes. Destinations are resolved against a fresh storage response before sending a provider operation; browser paths are never forwarded.

Action requests need `action` and a unique `requestId` (8–64 characters). Per-game actions also require `titleId` and the current `sourceKey`; copy/move need `destinationId`; cancellation needs the current numeric `jobId`. Scan, move and unmount require `confirmed:true`. Repeating the latest identical request ID returns its state without executing twice; reusing that ID for different input is a conflict. This is in-memory deduplication, not a durable replay log. Clients must not automatically replay commands after a lost response or restart.

The worker rechecks API v1 capabilities and current source identity before mutation. Copy/move require source-management support, an available unmounted source, supported progress, a writable destination and sufficient space after unfinished Orbit downloads. A move additionally requires copy, exact-source deletion, manual-source registration/removal, progress and cancellation capabilities. Orbit asks ShadowMount to copy, reads back and compares every file, registers the destination, rechecks the original source identity, then removes that exact source and its old registration. Verification or registration failures leave the original intact. `storageJob.state` reports `verifying` during readback and `finalizing` during registration/removal; cancellation is disabled once final removal starts. Mutating calls with an uncertain outcome are never replayed automatically. The provider performs its own filesystem checks. Downloads run beside a storage job: its remaining bytes count against downloads on the destination filesystem, and a download can't start or resume under its destination or source path (409, `Another file operation is using this.`). Storage jobs take turns with Files actions and the receiver. External clients can still start work independently. It polls the current provider job, discovers existing jobs after refresh/restart and never automatically retries a mutating POST. Unknown outcomes keep the storage job's turn until status can be confirmed. Completed downloads expose their saved `titleId`, `gameId`, `format` and original `path` for Library navigation, independent of catalogue changes. See [Library](library.md) for user-visible behavior and compatibility limits.

Manager status includes independent `managed` and `listed` flags for Payload Manager and Homebrew Launcher. `managed` reflects saved consent, while `listed` reports a present copy. Missing preferences default to no consent, including on upgrades. Invalid preferences set `preferencesError` and block external copy changes. Disabling integration preserves files and startup settings. Enabling Payload Manager auto-start requires integration opt-in; its global configuration is never written.

Update checks accept `{action:"check", automatic:true}` for opening or returning to the app. TV app checks (`/api/v1/tv-app`) accept the same flag with their own six-hour cooldown and `automaticCheckAfter`. Automatic calls share a six-hour in-memory cooldown across clients, observe the normal check/retry limits, and return the current status with 202 when no new request is needed. Manual checks retain the shorter cooldown. Status adds `updateAvailable` (a validated newer version) and `automaticCheckAfter` (Unix seconds). These checks never download an ELF, install it or stop Orbit. The browser remembers a dismissal for that version in its tab session, and newer versions can notify again.

Artwork requests (`/api/v1/art/...`) exist for the native TV app, which has no TLS stack of its own. Orbit never fetches a URL from the request: it looks up the game (its first visible option) and tries the catalogue's own HTTPS URLs in order: `cover` then `coverFallback`; for `hero`, `hero` then `heroFallback` for wide layouts and `heroFallback` alone for ambient ones. Fetches run on two workers so the HTTP thread never waits; responses must be WebP, PNG or JPEG by their content (the server's type is ignored), at most 12 MiB, over verified HTTPS with up to three HTTPS redirects. Images stay in an 8 MiB memory cache, least recently served first out; nothing is written to disk. The browser storefront still loads artwork directly.

The artwork proxies request width-limited variants from `image.api.playstation.com`: up to 600 pixels for covers and 1920 for backgrounds, preserving existing smaller widths and other query options. Other hosts retain their catalogue URLs. Orbit Zero keys its disk cache by the requested variant so older full-size copies are not reused. The native decoder checks PNG/JPEG dimensions and decoded size before allocating pixel buffers.


The TV app installer (`/api/v1/tv-app`) reads only the fixed feed `tv-app.json` in the public repository, a single object with `filename` (`orbit_store_ps4.pkg`), `version`, `url` (under the Orbit release downloads), `checksum` (SHA-256) and `size` in bytes, plus an optional `serviceVersion`: the download service inside that package. The TV app uses it to update both parts with one download, then starts that service itself when reopened. The native client omits the separate service download when the verified package contains it; **Close and reopen** closes the old UI. The reopened app completes the pending update through `stop` with `confirmed:true,resume:true`, then starts its bundled service through the local loader. A manual package replacement offers **Update download service** instead of automatically taking over an unrelated running session.

The PS4 package installer is authoritative: `installed` is derived from the console's package database (the title `ORBT00002` registered as installed), not from files. An installed package carrying Orbit's record in `/data/orbit-store/tv-app.json` (title id, version, checksum, installed path and file identity) counts as an Orbit-installed copy; without one it counts as a manual copy and needs `replace:true` to update. Folder installs under `ORBT00002/` and stray `orbit_store_ps4.pkg` files are detected on internal storage, USB0–7 and EXT0–7 (drive roots and `homebrew` directories), and the Library inventory is consulted; a folder copy, duplicate or blocked path refuses installation.

The package downloads over verified HTTPS with redirects limited to GitHub release hosts, stages under `/data/orbit-store/pkg/`, and is checked for exact size, SHA-256 and PS4 package magic before BGFT submission. `/data` must have space for the package plus headroom. `/data/orbit-store/tv-app-install.json` records submission intent before calling BGFT and the task ID afterward. A missing task, lost installer contact or service shutdown leaves the install `unconfirmed` and keeps the package and receipt. Another install is blocked while this receipt exists. Check resumes polling the saved task without downloading or submitting again, including after restart. If the task was not saved, Check can still confirm a registered installed package by its exact SHA-256 and size; otherwise it stays unconfirmed. A malformed receipt never authorizes replay.

Success records the version against the installed `app.pkg` identity before deleting the original, unchanged staged file and clearing the receipt. Changed staged files are kept. A known installer error clears the pending task but keeps the package. A PS4 refuses to install a title over itself, so for an Orbit-installed copy Orbit closes the TV app if it is open, removes the old copy and installs the new one, then opens it again if it was open; when it can't close or remove the old app, nothing is changed. The app's own files go with the old copy (on a PS4 they live in a disk image), so the new app takes its choices back from `/api/v1/tv-app/look`. Phases are `idle`, `checking`, `checked`, `downloading`, `verifying`, `installing`, `installed`, `unconfirmed` and `error`. A recovery check bypasses the feed cooldown; it cannot submit a new package.

A service update is not active just because it was saved. `runningVersion` identifies the current process, while `savedVersion` and `activationState: "saved"` identify a pending restart, including a same-version reinstall. For browser/service restart requests, without an answering ELF loader, `update-all` keeps the current service running and returns a restart notice. Users can stop Orbit and start `/data/orbit-store/orbit_store.elf` through Payload Manager. Manager copies are refreshed only when the owner has enabled their sync integration; a separately imported, unsynced copy can still start the older version. Status polling never opens an ELF-loader connection merely to test reachability.

### Provider browser session

Paired `GET /api/v1/browser` returns `{available, nativeDialogAvailable, active, id, title, state, message, jobId}`. States are `idle`, `opening`, `waiting`, `waiting-link`, `validating`, `queued`, `cancelled` and `failed`. AkiraBox and Vikingfile use `waiting-link` while the user completes verification and the provider prepares the file link. It also returns `vikingPass`, the state of a Vikingfile sign-in pass from another device (`none` when none is saved; see [Vikingfile sign-in pass](#vikingfile-sign-in-pass)). It never returns captured URLs, process IDs or browser bytes.

Paired `POST /api/v1/browser` accepts `{action:"start", releaseId, storageId, returnTarget?}` for a reviewed option with `browserUrl`, or `{action:"cancel", id}` for the current session. Optional `returnTarget` is `native` or `browser`. Browser return navigates to the fixed local Orbit URL after a verified job is persisted. Existing clients can still send the legacy boolean `returnToOrbit`; true means browser return. Supplying both fields or an unknown target returns 400. Older native clients return manually; relaunching an already-running title does not dismiss its browser overlay, so no title relaunch is attempted.

When `nativeDialogAvailable` is true, the native client can additionally send `nativeDialog:true` and a unique `clientId` (1–64 ASCII letters, digits, hyphens or underscores) with `returnTarget:"native"`. Status then echoes `clientId` and `dialogOpened`. Before acknowledgement, it also returns `pageUrl`, solely the selected catalogue option's public provider page. The native app opens this page in its own WebBrowserDialog and acknowledges `{action:"opened", id, clientId}`. This is idempotent for the active matching session. Capture waits for that acknowledgement, expires an abandoned opening after 30 seconds, and never launches a second system browser. Normal Origin/Host and pairing checks apply; arbitrary URLs cannot be submitted.

The owning native client can stop a failed attempt with `{action:"cancel", id, clientId, nativeFailure, errorCode?}`. `nativeFailure` must be `open`, `browser`, `timeout` or `connection`; optional `errorCode` is a signed 32-bit nonpositive integer. The service uses fixed messages, retains a negative platform code when supplied, and reports `failed` instead of a user cancellation. Unknown reasons or invalid codes return 400; foreign/stale sessions and already queued downloads return 409. Ordinary `{action:"cancel", id}` remains supported. Starting another session clears the previous failure. No provider page content or credentials are accepted or exposed through this report.

The native client closes only the dialog it opened, after observing `queued` with a nonempty `jobId`, or after failure/cancellation. It waits for the dialog to finish before restoring app input. User Back cancels the matching verification; a cancellation racing with a committed queue entry returns 409 and leaves the download intact. A lost start/acknowledgement response is reconciled by reading status, never by replaying creation. This lifecycle does not intercept provider popups or bypass human verification.

A start reserves one in-memory session, checks queue/storage eligibility and returns 202. A second start, stale acknowledgement/cancellation or unsupported platform returns 409. Once the matching file passes the one-byte response check, the queue persists its canonical provider route and pinned file identity. No verification session survives a payload restart. The native app polls through the same authenticated service and never creates a separate unvalidated download. Native dialog behavior requires console validation before release.

Catalogue responses add `browserAvailable` for supported wrapper options and `directAvailable` for directly transferable routes, and omit both `url` and `browserUrl`. Browser-only file-page options set `browserAvailable: true`, `directAvailable: false`, and `sourceVerification: file-metadata`. With direct delivery they require the authenticated browser flow; posting them to `/downloads` without a connected, supported TorBox delivery choice returns 409 with instructions and creates no job. `available` on the session status describes the native adapter separately from an option's metadata capability. The production desktop preview reports unavailable; compile-time local fixtures simulate capture for tests only. User verification and PS4 browser behavior require console validation before release.

### Local receiver

Orbit Zero uses the existing paired HTTP service. `GET /system` advertises `receiveProtocol:1` and `receiveAvailable`. Receiver requests require the normal bearer token; transfer ownership is pinned to that pairing.

- `POST /receive`: `{id, filename, size, storageId}` begins one transfer. IDs are 32 lowercase hex characters, filenames are plain names, and storage IDs resolve through Orbit's verified roots. Repeating an identical begin is idempotent.
- `GET /receive`: returns state, durable offset, maximum chunk size and availability. Optional `pipelineChunks:4`, `acceptedOffset` and `bufferedChunks` allow clients to overlap uploads with disk writes. `partialVerification:1` advertises verified partial recovery after a drive identity changes. Another pairing receives only `other-client`.
- `POST /receive/chunk`: binary body, at most 8 MiB, with `X-Orbit-Transfer`, `X-Orbit-Offset` and `X-Orbit-SHA256`. 202 means accepted by the disk worker, not yet durable. Uploads must start at `acceptedOffset`; poll status for the durable `offset`. The active and pending chunks share a four-chunk limit; 429 means the new chunk was not accepted and must be retried after space becomes available. Clients that do not use the optional pipeline can continue waiting for each chunk to become durable.
- `POST /receive/resume`: `{id}` validates the original drive and partial inode before retry. A published file is recovered only when its saved identity, size and full hash match.
- `POST /receive/finish`: `{id, sha256}` verifies the complete file, records publication intent and publishes without overwriting an existing file.
- `POST /receive/cancel`: `{id}` removes only the owned partial. Completed files are retained. Pausing is sender-side. A transfer that failed before writing anything is released by itself once its sender has been quiet for ten minutes; it then reports `cancelled` with `partialsRetained:true`.
- `POST /receive/bundle`: folder transfers, advertised as `receiveFolders:1` in `/system` and `folders:1` in `/receive`; `receiveProtocol` stays 1. `{action:"open", bundle, storageId, name, totalBytes}` creates a private `homebrew/.orbit-bundle-<id>/` after checking space and that `name` is unused. `POST /receive` with `{bundle, directory}` then sends each file into it as an ordinary transfer. `{action:"commit", bundle, files, totalBytes}` renames the folder to `name` only when the journal (`receive-bundle.json`) of finished files matches, never replacing an existing name. `{action:"cancel", bundle}` removes the staging folder; `{action:"abandon", bundle, confirmed:true}` releases it and keeps every file. While a folder is open, other transfers wait. Orbit downloads can continue when their paths and reserved space do not conflict. Status includes `bundle` for its owner and `bundleState:"other-client"` for other pairings.
- `POST /receive/abandon`: `{id, confirmed:true}` stops an unfinished transfer and releases its queue reservation without accessing either drive or deleting files. Available when `stopTransfer:1` is advertised. Only the original paired owner may stop its transfer; pending writes must settle first. The terminal state is `cancelled` with `partialsRetained:true`, preserved across restarts. Retrying is idempotent; completed files remain complete. A client must not describe retained files as removed.
- `POST /receive/recover`: `{ticket, code, confirmed:true, action}` recovers an abandoned pairing's unfinished transfer. Foreign status advertises `pairingRecovery:1`, `canRecoverPairing` and `recoveryWaitSeconds`; the requester-bound ticket appears after two minutes without owner activity and with disk work settled. Owner polls invalidate tickets. The current bearer token and PS5 pairing code are required, with pairing's attempt limit. `inspect` reveals saved file/bundle identities only after code verification. `claim` requires the inspected `id` and `bundle`, writes an atomic `receive-handoff.json` ownership record and preserves IDs, durable offsets and completed files across restarts. A nonempty claimed file sets `recoveryProofRequired`; no append, finish or bundle changes are allowed until `/receive/resume` verifies its full saved prefix SHA-256 (or complete-file hash for the last finished bundle file). Failed verification preserves all files. Explicit owned cancel can remove an unfinished partial; completed files are retained. The default/`stop` action retains files and releases reservations without resuming. Journal failures report an error.

When `partialVerification:1` is advertised, a failed resume or cancellation can be retried with `{id, prefixBytes, prefixSha256}`. `prefixBytes` must equal the current positive durable `offset`, and `prefixSha256` must cover those exact bytes in the computer's existing cache. Wait for the receiver to settle before reading the offset. The receiver verifies the entire saved prefix at the original storage ID/root before rebinding its filesystem identity. It rejects symlinks, hard links, destination-file conflicts, mismatched bytes and unavailable drives; it never adopts a file merely because its name matches. Verification is asynchronous and may take several minutes for a large partial. Keep the computer cache until cancellation is confirmed. A failed begin that never created a partial may cancel its empty reservation even when the drive is unavailable. Older receivers keep their existing `{id}` behavior.

An owned partial may be cancelled even if its size is below the saved resume offset; deletion still requires its original verified drive and file identity. If verification is impossible, including a missing computer cache or a remounted empty partial, explicit abandon releases the queue while retaining any remaining files. An empty checksum is never evidence of drive ownership. Stopped transfers cannot resume; a fresh download uses a new transfer ID and does not overwrite the retained partial.

The receiver keeps its destination descriptor open and batches checkpoints at 32 MiB or 250 ms, including a final checkpoint before completion. The worker flushes file bytes before advancing the journal. Accepted bytes in memory are not resumable progress. A failed chunk discards later pending chunks and resets acceptance to the durable prefix. Finish and cancel return 409 while pending disk work drains. Receiving runs beside regular downloads, which leave room for the bytes still to arrive and keep away from its destination name; it takes turns with Files actions and Library storage operations. Whole-file checksums are calculated while writing. Resume reconstructs the saved prefix; externally modified files invalidate the running checksum. No paths or executable commands can be supplied through this API.

Transfer partials start private (`0600` on permission-aware filesystems). After checksum verification, publication gives ordinary files read access for the game runtime (`0644`) and `.bin`, `.elf`, `.self`, `.prx` and `.sprx` files executable access (`0755`, case-insensitive). Directories require `0755`. Filesystems such as exFAT may expose fixed broader permissions; already accessible files do not require a chmod. Sender permissions and ownership are not copied. Before publishing a folder, the receiver also checks completed members from older, resumed transfers, repairing their permissions within the owned staging tree. Links, special files, other mounts and mismatched file counts or sizes prevent folder publication. Permission failures retain the files for retry and do not report completion. This does not scan or modify previously completed game folders.

Paired `POST /zero/probe` accepts `{releaseId}` and checks that catalogue source with a bounded one-byte request. `GET /zero/probe` exposes `releaseId`, `state` and `reachable`. It creates no download and changes no source setting. Desktop clients may use a successful matching result to choose a direct PS5 download for a new job.

Paired `POST /zero/link` (advertised as `zeroLinkProtocol:1` in `/system`, since 0.0.2) accepts `{releaseId, storageId, url}`: a download link Orbit Zero caught in its own Vikingfile, AkiraBox, DataNodes or 1fichier window, for the PS4 to download itself. The link must match the option's provider rules (for Vikingfile, a signed OVH storage link or a signed `/download/` link); otherwise the answer is 400 and nothing is requested. A valid request returns 202 and the check runs on its own thread: one bounded request confirms the file's name, size and identity, then the job is pinned to the chosen drive exactly as for a link caught in the console's own browser. The link never carries the console browser's cookies. One check runs at a time (409 while busy); 503 means the checker is unavailable. `GET /zero/link` returns `{id, releaseId, state:"idle"|"checking"|"queued"|"failed", message, jobId}` and never the link. Turning the source off, changing the option or stopping Orbit during the check queues nothing.

### Native Orbit Zero controls

Paired `POST /zero/companion` registers the desktop listener with `{action:"register",port,token}`. The numeric private IPv4 address is taken from the authenticated connection's peer, never a caller-provided host. Registration starts disabled; changing computers clears the opt-in. The native app enables/disables it using a loopback-only `{action:"enable",enabled}` request. `GET /zero/companion` is paired; only loopback clients receive the computer token. The atomic mode-0600 configuration survives an Orbit restart. Registration makes no network requests.

The native app talks to the registered computer on a worker thread. While enabled it reads catalogue/artwork there and starts new downloads using the desktop preference. Local source choices still filter the catalogue. Queue entries from the computer use a separate `zero-` namespace and retain independent internet and console-transfer progress. Console downloads continue to use the local service; a lost computer connection never silently starts a replacement console download. The computer accepts native requests only from its paired console address using the registered token and a separate native API. Tokens and source URLs are excluded from the native catalogue and queue responses.

In native Downloads, keeping a computer partial pauses both stages; deleting it cancels the transfer and deletes only its owned partial/cache. A completed console file is not removed by clearing the computer cache. Live console acceptance remains required for these development builds.

### Simultaneous downloads

`GET /api/v1/settings/downloads` returns `{concurrentDownloads: 1}` by default. Paired clients can POST the same property with an integer from 1 to 8. Invalid values return 400; failed persistence returns 503 and keeps the previous limit. The system response also includes `concurrentDownloads`. Lowering the limit does not interrupt active jobs; new jobs wait for a slot. Pause, cancel and resume still apply to one selected job. Archive extraction is serialized to bound decoder memory, while downloads can continue.

`downloadConnections` (default 8, 1–64) is how many connections one download uses when its source supports byte ranges: a new download is split into that many equal ranges, saved with the partial. Downloads running at once share up to 64: each gets at most 64 divided by `concurrentDownloads`, so eight at once keep eight each. A partial keeps its own split when the setting changes; the setting then only limits how many of its ranges download at once, and retries halve it as before. On a USB drive the file is still written in order, with that many requests in flight over an 8 MiB window. TorBox uses at most eight connections per game. Sources without range support still use one connection. An unfinished download with a split other than 1, 2, 4 or 8 is saved with schema 7, so an older build refuses the queue rather than misreading it; a finished one is saved as a single range, which every build reads.

### Download recovery

The same `/api/v1/settings/downloads` endpoint accepts partial updates to these fields. They are also returned by `/api/v1/system` and saved with the queue. Old state files retain the defaults. Invalid or unknown fields return 400; a save failure restores every previous value.

| Field | Default | Range | Meaning |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `downloadRetries` | 3 | 0–10 | Extra attempts after transient failures; 0 disables automatic retries. |
| `downloadRetryDelay` | 10 | 1–300 | Seconds before another attempt. A longer provider `Retry-After` takes precedence. |
| `downloadStallTimeout` | 60 | 15–600 | Observation window in seconds for sustained slow progress. |
| `downloadMinSpeed` | 1 | 1–1024 | Minimum aggregate download speed in KiB/s during that window. |

Each attempt snapshots the speed controls. Retry limits and delays are read when an attempt fails; an already scheduled wait keeps its deadline. Pause/cancel stop both transfer and pending recovery. Retries reopen from the writer's durable cursors, reduce simultaneous connections (for example, 8 → 4 → 2 → 1), and retain the original range layout and file validators. Slow disk backpressure is excluded from the speed watchdog. Provider throttling delays other queued jobs using that source (or TorBox), without blocking unrelated sources. Network errors alone do not delay other jobs.

Transient transport failures and HTTP 408/429/500/502/503/504 retry automatically. TorBox can resolve a fresh temporary link after 401/403/410, subject to the retry limit and unchanged file-identity checks. Other authentication failures, missing files, invalid ranges, changed identity and disk errors remain actionable errors. A captured provider link that expires keeps the partial file and asks the user to refresh the link. HTTP 206 itself is a normal partial-file response, not a failure. Brief retry waits retain the game's queue slot; longer provider cooldowns let other eligible games proceed.

Orbit Zero exposes the same fields through its authenticated desktop-only `/api/download-settings` endpoint for **computer downloads**. Its settings are separate from the PS5 service. It retains its ordered durable-prefix resume checks, shares up to 64 active connections across computer downloads and caps TorBox at eight per game. Fresh TorBox link resolution after a connection failure does not guarantee a different CDN server, and never switches a raw partial download to a ZIP representation. These options do not control PS5 transfer retries or archive extraction.

### Pairing recovery for Orbit Zero

`GET /api/v1/system` advertises `receivePairingRecovery: 1`. A freshly paired desktop may send its former 64-character secret in `X-Orbit-Previous-Pairing` for `/api/v1/receive` requests to retain ownership of its existing receiver job. Every request still requires the new valid bearer token. The former secret alone is never authorization. The desktop verifies saved partial bytes against its retained computer copy before resuming, and requires a fresh on-screen code plus confirmation when pairing has been reset.

## Saved filters

Browse's filters, sort and search can be saved under a name and applied later in the browser or the TV app. They are kept in Orbit's state on the PS4 beside the favourites, so every paired app sees the same ones, and they survive restarts.

Each saved filter is `{id, name, page, filters, savedAt}`. `page` is `games` (Browse) or `addons` (Add-ons); each page lists only its own. `filters` is complete and checked: `query` (up to 200 bytes), `source`, `format`, `tags` and `genres` (up to 32 distinct strings each), `region`, `platform` (`""`, `ps4`, `ps5`), `size` (`""`, `small`, `medium`, `large`, `huge`), `collection` (`all`, `favorites`), `hideInstalled`, `sort` (`release`, `added`, `title`, `title-desc`, `size`, `size-desc`) and `addonType`. Missing filters take their defaults; a wrong type or value is refused with 400. Older saved filters without `genres` use an empty list (all genres). Genre choices use the game's detail metadata, merge equivalent labels, and appear when at least ten games in the full catalogue have that genre; active search and other filters do not remove choices.

Names are 1 to 40 characters without leading or trailing spaces. Saving under a name the page already has, in any letter case, replaces that filter and keeps its ID. There are at most 50 saved filters (409 once full; replacing still works). Deleting an unknown ID is 404. A save that can't be written to the state file is 503 and changes nothing. Applying a saved filter happens in the app; values the catalogue no longer offers stay as they were saved.

Since 0.0.3, saved filters also accept `minimumScore` (`""`, `60`, `70`, `80` or `90`, as strings), `playtimeRange` (`""`, `under5`, `5to10`, `10to20`, `20to40` or `40plus`), and `playStyle` (`main`, `extras` or `completionist`). Sort additionally accepts `score`, `score-desc`, `time` and `time-desc`. Missing score and playtime filters are empty; missing play style uses `main`. Unknown metadata is excluded only when the corresponding filter is active and sorts last.

## Files

A place is a drive ID from `/storage` and a `path` from the drive's top: names joined by `/`, `""` for the top. Names starting with a dot (including Orbit's `.orbit-` working files), `$RECYCLE.BIN`, `System Volume Information`, and `user` and `ps4` at the top of extended storage (`ext0`–`ext7`) are hidden and refused as paths, as are empty, `.` and `..` names. Every path is walked one name at a time with `O_NOFOLLOW` on the drive's own device; links, special files and other mounts are skipped.

`POST /files/list` returns `{storageId, path, entries, truncated}`. Each entry is `{name, folder, type, sizeBytes, modifiedAt, locked}`: `type` is `folder`, `game` (a folder with `eboot.bin` or `sce_sys/param.json`), `archive` (`.zip`, `.7z`, `.rar`), `package` (`.pkg`, `.fpkg`), `image` (`.exfat`, `.ffpkg`, `.ffpfsc`) or `file`; `sizeBytes` is `null` for folders; `locked` is `""` or why it can't be changed: `orbit` (Orbit's state folder or one holding it), `download` (an unfinished download's file), `install` (a package the PS4 is installing), `game` (a game ShadowMount has installed or mounted, or a folder holding it), `busy` (the running operation's source or destination). The first 2,000 entries are listed; `truncated` says there were more. 400 for a bad path, 404 for a missing drive or folder.

`POST /files/action`:

| Action | Fields | Result |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `folder` | `path` (the folder), `name` | 200. 409 if the name exists, 400 for a name an exFAT drive can't store or one starting with a dot |
| `rename` | `path` (the entry), `name` | 200, in the same folder; a case change is allowed. 409 if locked or the name exists |
| `copy`, `move` | `path`, `toStorageId`, `toPath` (the destination folder) | 202. A copy into a folder that has the name gets `name (2)`, `name (3)`…; a move refuses an existing name. Moving within a drive renames; across drives it copies, then removes the originals. 409 into itself, into its own folder (move), or when locked |
| `delete` | `path` | 202. Removes a folder's whole tree |
| `unpack` | `path` (a ZIP, 7z or RAR file) | 202. As downloads extract: never replaces a name. State `password` when no known password opens it |
| `install` | `path` (a PKG file, game image or game folder) | 202. Creates an installation receipt; packages go to the PS4's installer, images and folders to ShadowMount (a scan for `homebrew`, `manual/add` by path elsewhere when ShadowMount offers `add_manual_source`) |
| `measure` | `path` (a folder) | 202. `sizeBytes` when complete |
| `pause`, `resume` | `id` | 200. Copies and moves only, not while a move removes its originals |
| `cancel` | `id` | 200. Not for installs, or while a move removes its originals |
| `password` | `id`, `password` | 200 for an unpack in state `password` |

One operation runs at a time (409 while another runs). `/files/status` reports it as `{id, action, state, name, storageId, path, toStorageId, toPath, processedBytes, totalBytes, speed, error, sizeBytes}`; `state` is `measuring`, `running`, `paused`, `password`, `complete`, `failed` or `cancelled`. Copies are written in a private `.orbit-copy-<id>` folder in the destination and appear only when complete; free space is checked first (plus 16 MiB), and a stopped copy's staging folder is removed. Mutating Files actions take turns with the receiver and Library operations (409 while one runs) but not with downloads. A copy or unpack's remaining bytes count against downloads on its filesystem, and a download can't start or resume under a path the action writes or removes. Measurement is read-only. Copy workers verify the source tree identity before and after reading it and refuse changed sources without publishing the staged copy or deleting originals. Staging cleanup only removes Orbit-owned names with the expected operation ID pattern. Operations aren't saved: after a restart `/files/status` is `null`.

`POST /files/link` checks that the entry is a file and returns a ticket URL. The ticket names the file as it was (device, inode, size and modification time) and serves it for five minutes, also for `Range` requests (`bytes=a-b`, `a-`, `-n`; 416 otherwise), with `Content-Disposition: attachment` and `Cache-Control: no-store`. Up to 16 links are kept.

## Archive.org sign-in

Archive.org serves some files only to signed-in accounts. Without a sign-in, `archive.org/download/…` redirects to a storage server that answers 403. Paired `POST /api/v1/archive-account` with `{action:"sign-in", email, password}` sends the email and password once to Archive.org's login service (`https://archive.org/services/xauthn/?op=login`) and wipes them. Orbit keeps only the two session cookies Archive.org returns (`logged-in-user` and `logged-in-sig`) and the account's screen name, in `archive-account.json` (mode 0600) in Orbit's state directory. Archive.org's other credentials in the reply, such as its API keys, are discarded. The email must be 3–254 printable characters with an `@`, and the password 1–256 characters without control characters. The request waits for Archive.org for up to seven seconds. Errors are fixed sentences; Archive.org's own text is never relayed.

Downloads from the `archive` source carry the session through libcurl's cookie engine, scoped to `.archive.org` over HTTPS, so a redirect to any other host never receives it. TorBox deliveries never use it. The Orbit Zero source check (`/zero/probe`) uses it too, so a login-only file counts as reachable on a signed-in console.

When Archive.org answers 401 or 403, Orbit asks `https://archive.org/metadata/<item>/is_dark`. A taken-down item fails with "Archive.org has taken this game down. Choose another source." Otherwise, a signed-out console fails with "This file needs an Archive.org account. Sign in to Archive.org in App settings, then retry.", and a signed-in one with "Archive.org didn't allow this file for your account. Sign in to Archive.org again in App settings, or choose another source." None of these are retried automatically; Retry after signing in continues the download.

`{action:"sign-out"}` deletes `archive-account.json`. The catalogue does not mark login-only files: a download finds out when Archive.org refuses it.

## Vikingfile sign-in pass

Vikingfile's sign-in page runs Cloudflare's human check in the browser, and some PS4 browsers (reported on firmware 9.00) freeze or close on it. As a second way to sign in, the user signs in on vikingfile.com in a browser on another device and pastes that browser's `PHPSESSID` cookie value into Orbit. Orbit never submits Vikingfile's sign-in form or its human check itself.

Paired `POST /api/v1/viking-pass` with `{action:"save", pass}` accepts the value alone, `PHPSESSID=value`, quotes and a trailing `;`, after trimming spaces. The value must be 16–256 letters, digits, `,` or `-`. Orbit asks `https://vikingfile.com/` with the pass and saves it only when the page shows a signed-in account, in `viking-pass.json` (mode 0600) in Orbit's state directory. A pass Vikingfile shows as signed out is refused with 409 and nothing is saved. The request waits for Vikingfile for up to six seconds. The pass is never returned, logged, put in diagnostics or saved in the queue.

When a Vikingfile download asks for a link, a saved pass is tried first. If Vikingfile shows it signed in, the job is marked as using the pass (`vikingContext` 3 in private queue state) and its link check, download and resumes send only the pass, as a host-only `vikingfile.com` cookie over HTTPS, so the storage server it redirects to never receives it. If Vikingfile shows the pass signed out, Orbit uses the PS4 browser's own Vikingfile sign-in as before and `vikingPass` becomes `signed-out`. After a restart the pass is `unknown` until a download or `{action:"check"}` asks Vikingfile again. `{action:"forget"}` deletes `viking-pass.json`. A download that was using the pass then fails at its next request with "Vikingfile sign-in is unavailable. Sign in again and refresh the download link.", as when the PS4 browser's sign-in is gone.

### Archive passwords

`POST /api/v1/downloads/:id/archive-password` (paired) accepts `{ "password": "…" }` for an errored or paused archive job whose complete downloaded archive is still present. The password must contain 1–128 UTF-8 bytes and no control characters. A successful request queues extraction of that existing archive, without downloading it again. Jobs expose `canEnterArchivePassword` for the UI: true only when the archive's last extraction stopped because no password opened it, not after other extraction failures.
